Souls Under the Altar
SOHLZ UN-der thee AWL-ter
n. phr. (the martyrs seen at the opening of the fifth seal, crying How long)
Greek hypokatō tou thysiastēriou tas psychas — hypokatō, underneath; thysiastērion, the altar of sacrifice; the place is significant, for the blood of a sacrifice was poured out at the base of the altar.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

“And when he had opened the fifth seal, I saw under the altar the souls of them that were slain for the word of God, and for the testimony which they held: And they cried with a loud voice, saying, How long, O Lord, holy and true, dost thou not judge and avenge our blood on them that dwell on the earth?” They are given white robes and told to rest yet for a little season, until their fellowservants should be killed as they were. The location carries the doctrine: the blood of the sacrifices was poured at the foot of the altar, and these are souls whose lives were poured out as an offering, which is exactly how Paul speaks of his own death. Several things follow. The martyrs are conscious, vocal, and in heaven immediately after death, which settles the intermediate state. Their prayer is for judgment and vengeance, and it is not rebuked but answered with a white robe and a timetable — so the imprecations of the Psalter are not a lower morality the New Testament outgrew. And the answer given is that a number must yet be filled, which means the church's suffering is measured and counted by God. Nothing here suggests the martyrs are to be prayed to; they are the ones praying.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): Altar, an elevated place on which sacrifices were offered. Soul, the spiritual, immortal part of man. I saw under the altar the souls of them that were slain, Revelation 6:9, the martyrs at the opening of the fifth seal.

expand to see more

Altar, an elevated place or structure on which sacrifices were offered to God.

Soul, the spiritual and immortal part of man, distinct from the body.

Greek thysiastērion, the altar of sacrifice, at whose base blood was poured.

Greek psychē, the soul; here conscious, vocal, and in heaven.

They are told to rest yet for a little season, Revelation 6:11.

Key Scripture

Rev 6:9 — "And when he had opened the fifth seal, I saw under the altar the souls of them that were slain for the word of God, and for the testimony which they held:"

Rev 6:10 — "And they cried with a loud voice, saying, How long, O Lord, holy and true, dost thou not judge and avenge our blood on them that dwell on the earth?"

Rev 6:11 — "And white robes were given unto every one of them; and it was said unto them, that they should rest yet for a little season, until their fellowservants also and their brethren, that should be killed as they were, should be fulfilled."

Rev 20:4 — "And I saw thrones, and they sat upon them, and judgment was given unto them: and I saw the souls of them that were beheaded for the witness of Jesus, and for the word of God, and which had not worshipped the beast, neither his image, neither had received his mark upon their foreheads, or in their hands; and they lived and reigned with Christ a thousand years."

Modern Corruption

The passage is pressed into the invocation of saints and the cult of relics beneath altars, and from the other side emptied by soul-sleep, which cannot account for souls that speak.

expand to see more

Rome's practice of placing relics beneath altars and of invoking the martyrs as intercessors has long appealed to this verse. The text gives no warrant for either. These souls pray to God, not to the living, and no one in the chapter prays to them; their cry is a plea for divine judgment, and the answer comes from God alone. Scripture directs prayer to God through the one Mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus, and the New Testament's only priesthood besides His is that of all believers. A doctrine of saintly mediation built on a verse in which the saints themselves are petitioners inverts the passage.

The denial of the conscious intermediate state must handle the verse no better. Souls that cry with a loud voice, are addressed, are given robes, and are told to wait a little season are not asleep or non-existent. The principle to recover is the one the Reformed confessions state: the souls of the righteous, being made perfect in holiness, are received into the highest heavens, where they behold the face of God, waiting for the full redemption of their bodies. And with it recover the martyrs' prayer itself, which the church has grown shy of — How long, O Lord, holy and true — a petition for justice that God answers and does not reprove.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek thysiastērion, the altar at whose base sacrificial blood was poured; psychē, soul — lives poured out as an offering, conscious and crying for judgment.

expand to see more

Greek thysiastērion, the altar of sacrifice; blood was poured at its base.

Greek psychē, the soul, here conscious, vocal, and clothed in white.

Greek sphazō, to slay or slaughter, used of a sacrificial killing.

Greek heōs pote, how long — the martyrs' cry, Revelation 6:10.

Compare Paul poured out as an offering, 2 Timothy 4:6, and Philippians 2:17.

Usage

"I saw under the altar the souls of them that were slain"

"How long, O Lord, holy and true"

"that they should rest yet for a little season"
